title: Peoria Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Peoria wells have a 315 ft median depth; see local yields, water levels, drilling costs, permits and risks before buying.
h1: Peoria, Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Buying land near Peoria means evaluating the well, not just the house or acreage. Records for permitted wells within 5 miles show a wide range of drilling conditions: reported depths run from shallow wells to 1,110 feet, with a median of 315 feet. Most reported yields fall between 10 and 13 gallons per minute.

This page uses Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records for Peoria and nearby plains communities including Deer Trail, Byers and Strasburg. The records are useful for setting expectations, but a neighboring well is not a guarantee for your lot. Get the permit, construction, pump and water-quality history before you commit.

sections.heading: Peoria wells can range from shallow to very deep
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Peoria is 315 feet. The middle half runs from 103 to 620 feet, so two nearby properties can require very different drilling bids. The 90th percentile is 700 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 1,110 feet.

The depth mix shows why an average estimate can mislead: 23% of wells are under 100 feet, 20% are between 100 and 300 feet, 29% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 27% are over 600 feet. Permits identify Denver Basin aquifer wells throughout this area, including Arapahoe and Laramie Fox Hills records, along with unnamed or fractured-bedrock entries.

sections.heading: Most Peoria wells report usable production
sections.html:
Among the 274 wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 10.0 to 13.0 gallons per minute. That is a stronger production pattern than many rural buyers assume, but it is still a well-by-well result rather than a promise for an un drilled site.

75% of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 23% report more than 15 gallons per minute. The records show 0% under 1 gallon per minute and 2% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Ask for the actual well test and pump information, not only a listing description.

sections.heading: Recorded water levels do not show a simple decline
sections.html:
Only 57 records report a static water level, so this part of the dataset is much smaller than the depth and yield samples. The median depth to water is 80 feet, with the middle half from 60 to 175 feet below the surface.

The decade comparison does not suggest a dropping water table in these records. The median measurement was 112 feet below ground in the 2010s and 80 feet in the 2020s. Those measurements come from different wells and sites, so they should not be treated as a continuous monitoring station. A driller or pump contractor should measure the static and pumping levels on the property being considered.

sections.heading: Peoria permit activity and the drillers in the records
sections.html:
Permit activity increased sharply in the local records during the 1990s and 2000s: 112 permits were issued in the 1990s and 210 in the 2000s. The records include 57 permits from the 2010s and 53 from the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025.

The most frequently listed driller is Crandall Drilling & Pump Service, including Crandall Jr. and Howard H., with 132 records. Don Eastwood Drilling Inc. appears on 65, and Can America Drilling, Inc., including Arde, Wayne A., appears on 56. Permit history can help identify nearby construction patterns, but confirm who would handle your new well today.

sections.heading: A median-depth Peoria well can cost this much
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 315-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $15,800 to $22,000. That is drilling only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $21,800 to $34,000 at the median depth. A deeper-than-median hole can move outside that range, especially when the site needs difficult access or additional construction work. Request a written bid that separates drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical and testing.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic spacing and dry-hole risk
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 18 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not establish contamination at a particular parcel, and the mapped records are not a substitute for testing. Have the well water tested before closing and after construction as appropriate.

Low-yield and dry-hole risk still matters even though the reported yield distribution is generally solid. Review nearby permits for depth, aquifer, yield and static level. On a buildable lot, confirm the well location, septic area, access for a rig, setbacks, casing and grout requirements, and electrical route. Colorado well permits and household-use rules control what can be pumped and used; an augmentation plan may matter in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: What to do before buying or building near Peoria
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare several nearby permitted wells rather than relying on the countywide median. Properties near Deer Trail and Byers may provide useful context, but the closest well is the better comparison when its geology and intended use are similar. Check whether the existing well is permitted, constructed, tested and equipped for the home you plan to occupy.

For a new build, make the well and septic layout part of the site plan before excavation. Budget against the local finished-system estimate, while allowing for a depth outside the 103-to-620-foot middle range. Confirm household, stock or irrigation use with the permit. A licensed driller should evaluate the site, and a water-quality professional should test the source before you make the well part of your closing decision.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Peoria, Colorado?
faq.a: Permitted wells within 5 miles of Peoria have a median reported depth of 315 feet. The middle half ranges from 103 to 620 feet. The 90th percentile is 700 feet, and the deepest record is 1,110 feet, so a site-specific estimate matters.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Peoria?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 315-foot median depth, drilling is estimated at $15,800 to $22,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $21,800 to $34,000. Deeper drilling can raise the total.

faq.q: How much water do Peoria wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 13.0 gallons per minute. 75% of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 23% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Peoria, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or nearby well. Within about 10 miles, records map 18 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory before closing and investigate any nearby environmental record.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Peoria?
faq.a: The available records do not show a simple decline. Median static water level was 112 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 80 feet in the 2020s. However, only 57 wells report static levels, and the measurements come from different sites, so they are not a continuous trend record.
